title: Ethiopia and Eritrea Sever Diplomatic Ties as Northern Ethiopia Fighting Escalates
summary:
Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations — a major break between two neighboring countries in the Horn of Africa. The move comes as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict.

On Thursday, Ethiopia announced it was closing its embassy in Asmara, Eritrea's capital, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave within 48 hours. Ethiopia accused them of activities that threatened national security. Eritrea responded by cutting all diplomatic ties, saying Ethiopia's decision left it "no option but to reciprocate in kind." Its foreign ministry called the expulsion "astounding" and warned of "negative corollaries."

The diplomatic confrontation followed powerful explosions overnight in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia's capital, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters. More than 50 people have been killed since heavy fighting resumed last week.

Ethiopian federal forces are battling fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of Tigray, Afar and Amhara. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting a new rebel alliance — an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied. Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated goal is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.

The split marks a dramatic reversal from 2018, when Abiy restored relations with Asmara after two decades of hostility. That rapprochement helped earn him the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019. The current hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated about 600,000 people died during that two-year conflict.

Ethiopia also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, giving him 48 hours to leave, according to state media. The government gave no public reason. Relations with Egypt have been strained for years over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a huge hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile. Egypt, which relies heavily on the Nile for water, has long worried about the dam's impact on its water supply.
why_it_matters: A wider war in the Horn of Africa would sit right next to the Red Sea, one of the world's busiest shipping routes, and could push up prices and destabilise a region where millions already depend on food aid. It also shows how quickly a celebrated peace deal can collapse when underlying disputes are never resolved.

background_read: Ethiopia and Eritrea are neighbours in the Horn of Africa, the region on the continent's eastern edge. Eritrea (a small country on the Red Sea that won independence from Ethiopia in 1993) fought a devastating border war with Ethiopia from 1998 to 2000, and the two states stayed locked in hostility for nearly two decades afterwards.

That changed in 2018, when Abiy Ahmed (Ethiopia's prime minister, in office since 2018) signed a peace deal with Eritrea and won the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize for it. The goodwill did not last: in 2020 war broke out in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had dominated Ethiopian politics before Abiy took power.

Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian forces during that war, which the African Union (a continental body representing African countries, headquartered in Addis Ababa) helped mediate to an end in 2022. Estimates of the death toll in the Tigray war run into the hundreds of thousands, and many of the underlying disputes were never fully settled.

Separately, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (a giant hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile) has poisoned Ethiopia's relations with Egypt, which sits downstream and depends on the Nile for almost all of its fresh water. That long-running water dispute is one reason the region's diplomacy is so tangled.

perspectives.description: Ethiopia frames the expulsions as a national-security measure, saying the diplomats it ordered out were engaged in activities that threatened the state. Standing firm against Eritrea and the TPLF-led alliance may also strengthen Abiy's domestic support while federal forces are stretched across three regions.

Critics warn that cutting ties removes the few remaining channels for talking at exactly the moment when explosions are being heard in Addis Ababa and more than 50 people have died. Regional analysts also fear Eritrea could be pulled deeper into the fighting, dragging the wider Horn of Africa in with it.

The break is a striking reversal of 2018, when Abiy won the Nobel Peace Prize for reopening relations with Asmara. The Horn's recent history is full of such swings: the 1998–2000 border war ended in a frozen stalemate, and even the 2022 Tigray peace deal, after a conflict estimated to have killed about 600,000 people, has not settled the underlying political disputes.

Much depends on whether the African Union or other mediators can restart talks and whether the rebel alliance holds together or fractures. At the same time, Ethiopia is managing a separate confrontation with Egypt over the GERD dam, which makes de-escalation on any single front harder to achieve.
